requirement_text: We require the SAT or the ACT from first year and transfer applicants. We accept both the paper and digital SAT. We do not require the ACT writing or science sections or the SAT optional essay. MIT does not have cut off or recommended scores for the ACT or SAT, as scores are evaluated within an applicant's context. If you take the same test multiple times, MIT primarily considers the highest score achieved in each section (superscore). Applicants self-report scores on the application; MIT verifies scores upon enrollment and scores cannot be redacted from an application after submission.

limitations: MIT does not publish a minimum/cutoff score — this is a binary submission requirement (a score must be reported), not a numeric threshold to compare a student's score against. MIT grants full review without presumption of unpreparedness if an applicant cannot test due to 'disaster or disruption' or because SAT/ACT are 'unavailable or unsafe' in their region (per the 2022-03-28 reinstatement announcement) — check this carveout before evaluating a missing score as not_met.
researcher_notes: TRAP CHECK (test-optional/required conflict, the top risk flagged for this research pass): MIT suspended its SAT/ACT requirement for the 2020-21 and 2021-22 cycles during the pandemic (mitadmissions.org/blogs/entry/we-are-suspending-our-sat-act-requirement-for-the-2020-2021-application-cycle/ and the 2021-2022 sequel), then reinstated it on 2022-03-28, first applying to 'the prospective Class of 2027 (and beyond)' — MIT's graduating-class label for students entering Fall 2023, NOT to be confused with this record's schema cycle_year=entry-year convention. Checked mitadmissions.org/apply/firstyear/testing/ (404, page moved), /apply/firstyear/tests-scores/, /help/faq-topic/testing/, and catalog.mit.edu/mit/undergraduate-education/admissions for a stale contradicting test-optional page still live — NONE found. All current pages state the requirement in the present tense as of retrieval (2026-08-21) with no hedging. The two 2020/2021 'suspending' blog posts are dated historical news announcements bound to named past cycles, not live pages presenting themselves as current policy, so this is NOT recorded as CONFLICTING_EVIDENCE — MIT's status is unambiguous, matching the brief's prediction that MIT (an early reinstater) would likely be clean. cycle_year left null per this batch's discipline of only setting cycle_year when the SOURCE PAGE itself names a cycle; none of MIT's current requirement pages do (no 'Class of 2031' or '2026-2027' label found on the live pages), even though the fact is empirically cycle-sensitive (it has changed by cycle before). The reinstatement announcement itself is cited only as historical corroboration, not as the source_url, since the live requirements page is the operative current source.

requirement_text: The MIT first-year application includes four main essay questions (approximately 100-200 words each): what field of study appeals to you most right now and what led to this interest; a time you did something differently than what was expected of you; a way you have positively impacted your community; and how you managed a significant challenge or setback. It also includes four short-response questions (approximately 40-50 words each): what you do just for fun; someone you admire and why; a topic you could discuss for hours; and whether you consider yourself more of a generalist or a specialist. One optional free-text box is provided for additional information.

requirement_text: Interviews are not a required part of the MIT application. Interviews are conducted from October through November for Early Action and December through January for Regular Action. MIT has limited interview availability (over 3,500 alumni volunteer Educational Counselors worldwide) and cannot offer an interview to every applicant. If your interview is waived, it will not put you at a disadvantage in the admissions process, and the admissions committee will be aware that MIT was unable to offer you an interview.

requirement_text: MIT's need-blind admissions process ensures that you will not be disadvantaged in the admissions process because of your financial need. Our admissions process is need-blind for all students, foreign and domestic. MIT is one of only nine colleges in the U.S. that is both need-blind and full-need for all of its undergraduate students, domestic and international.

requirement_text: MIT's Early Action program is both nonbinding and nonrestrictive. There's no difference in the review process or criteria used for admission in EA versus RA, and thus no advantage or disadvantage to applying for either round, aside from learning your decision earlier. MIT does not offer an Early Decision program — only Early Action and Regular Action exist. All students, regardless of citizenship or location, may apply for either the EA or RA round; an applicant may only apply in one round per entry year.

researcher_notes: BINDING/EXCLUSIVITY COMPANION RECORD, per the research brief's instruction to treat early-round exclusivity terms as eligibility-affecting information, not just a date. Verified directly (not assumed) that MIT does not offer Early Decision at all — per the brief's instruction not to invent an ED record that doesn't exist, no ED record was created. Because MIT's EA is confirmed nonrestrictive, an applicant may apply EA to MIT while also applying ED or EA to other private universities in the same cycle — unlike Restrictive/Single-Choice Early Action programs offered by some other universities, which forbid that. requirement_text: All students apply to MIT for general admission and select a major (course) at the end of the first year with help from their first-year advisor; therefore all applicants must meet the same test requirements.
